decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;TL;DR: PopClip, Raycast, BetterTouchTool, Keyboard Maestro, Apple Shortcuts, Supercharge, and ExtraBar; concrete daily uses for each, not feature dumps. For people already comfortable on macOS who've hit a specific friction point (clipboard, mouse buttons, background-app switching) and want the tool that kills it.&lt;/p&gt;&lt;p&gt;One of the perks of working on a Mac: with a few painful exceptions, whatever workflow itch you have, some app already scratches it. The longer you're in this ecosystem, the more tweaks and hacks you accumulate, until the line between "native" and "third-party" gets blurry — the good ones just start to feel built in. These are apps I recommend constantly without always explaining why. So here they are: a few Mac powerhouses, and the specific things I actually use them for.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Popclip&lt;/strong&gt; Performs actions on selected text&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/popclip-a-must-have-productivity-app"&gt;PopClip - A Must Have Productivity App&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Either script or use ChatGPT to write your own extensions for any website you search frequently. I have extensions for GoodReads, Anna's Archive and Kagi.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Send text to Terminal, iTerm or Ghostty&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Add text to the clipboard without erasing what's already there — works multiple times in succession, so you can build up a batch before pasting&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Raycast&lt;/strong&gt; Spotlight Replacement with plugin architecture&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/how-to-get-the-most-from-raycast"&gt;How to Get The Most from Raycast&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Even with the huge selection of standalone clipboard managers, I always fall back to Raycast's for searchable categories, editing clips, pinning clips and more&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Shortcut combo for Kagi, my search engine of choice (⌘+k, enter a search term, press enter)&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Built in emoji picker is 🔥&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;BetterTouchTool&lt;/strong&gt; Input controlled Mac automation&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/better-touch-tool-favorite"&gt;Better Touch Tool Favorites&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;No need for a separate app to program my 6-button Logitech mouse — extras include instant Mission Control, show-all-spaces, an application switcher, and a pie menu&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Completely replaced Elgato Stream Deck software (a security nightmare) with BTT, and it works even better&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Uses typed strings for triggers, not just hotkey combos, and it lets you use the Fn (globe) key — something Keyboard Maestro doesn't expose. I've programmed double-taps of all my modifier keys for special functions&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Keyboard Maestro&lt;/strong&gt; 30 different triggers for Mac automations&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/keyboard-maestro-the-app-that-makes-everything-better-tips-for-the-for-the-automation-curious"&gt;Keyboard Maestro, The App That Makes Everything Better - Tips for the Automation Curious&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Batch open and batch close apps to switch contexts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Launch anything on a schedule with time of day triggers&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Mount and unmount selected groups of network drives with a hotkey&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Apple Shortcuts&lt;/strong&gt; Programming for non-programmers&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/enhance-apple-shortcuts-with-these-apps"&gt;Enhance Apple Shortcuts with These Apps&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;&lt;li value="1"&gt;Even more scheduled tasks:&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Create an Obsidian daily note and add weather and calendar events&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Build a daily CSV that combines web history from Safari and Firefox into one document&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Text every person in my address book on their birthday&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Run a weekly backup of all my shortcuts&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;/li&gt;&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;macOS&lt;/strong&gt; Many, many undocumented tweaks&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Make the dock disappear with no delay&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Make the library folder in my home directory always visible&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Change the default screenshot file type to jpg&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Supercharge&lt;/strong&gt; Huge collection of useful system tweaks&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/using-supercharge"&gt;Using Supercharge&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Close all open apps&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Close everything in Notification Center at once&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Backup and restore the settings for any app, super useful with new computers&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Find out what keyboard shortcuts are in use&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;ExtraBar&lt;/strong&gt; Puts anything you want to do into one always-available menu&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/extra-bar-gets-extra-features"&gt;WIP — Extra Bar Gets Extra Features&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Pick any running application from a list — including background ones — and restart it&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Mark all unread mail as read in Fastmail&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;I'm currently running three displays and sixteen virtual desktops, and I keep a folder in ExtraBar with a shortcut to each one&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Who this list is for&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You already know your way around macOS and you're not looking for training wheels. You've hit some specific friction — clipboard chaos, a mouse with buttons doing nothing, shortcuts that only run when you remember to open the app — and you want the tool that kills it, not a tour of System Settings.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Who it's not for&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you're still getting comfortable with the Mac basics, most of this will feel like solving problems you don't have yet. Raycast's clipboard categories and BetterTouchTool's Fn-key double-taps are answers to annoyances you haven't accumulated. Start with the stock apps; come back when something specific starts bothering you.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Why these and not the alternatives&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Every one of these replaces something clunkier: BTT over Stream Deck's software, Raycast over Spotlight and a half-dozen single-purpose clipboard managers, ExtraBar over hunting through Mission Control for a background app. None of them are novelties. They're in daily rotation because pulling any one out would put a specific annoyance back in my life immediately.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=7%20Mac%20utilities%20I" d fight to keep and what i actually use them for another apps list style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

For people already comfortable on macOS who've hit a specific friction point (clipboard, mouse buttons, background-app switching) and want the tool that kills it.

One of the perks of working on...</summary>

    <link rel="alternate" type="text/html" href="https://appaddict.app/post/2026-07-18"/>
    <title>CurrentKey, Removing Mac Friction Points with Space Naming and ScreenTime Info You Can Actually Use</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpeg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" srcset="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNnpUQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--4344395abcd90501067068352ba271205e1f1371/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQzRBRnBBdUFCT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--278b8a01e32dcdca3afe205e3ef51dea30581376/63848.jpeg 480w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNnpUQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--4344395abcd90501067068352ba271205e1f1371/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0lBTnBBaUFET2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--6b540d5bfcfeca9a1dc6d345f6876757413a9f8d/63848.jpeg 800w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNnpUQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--4344395abcd90501067068352ba271205e1f1371/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0FBUnBBZ0FFT2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--c3a30915df96623eeb10e1076dd39fd8d058239f/63848.jpeg 1024w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNnpUQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--4344395abcd90501067068352ba271205e1f1371/63848.jpeg" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBNnpUQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--4344395abcd90501067068352ba271205e1f1371/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lKYW5CbFp3WTZCa1ZVT2hSeVpYTnBlbVZmZEc5ZmJHbHRhWFJiQjJrQ0lBTnBBaUFET2dwellYWmxjbnNIT2d4eGRXRnNhWFI1YVZrNkNuTjBjbWx3VkE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoidmFyaWF0aW9uIn19--6b540d5bfcfeca9a1dc6d345f6876757413a9f8d/63848.jpeg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Here are two Mac friction points:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;It's been 16 years since Mission Control was released, and "Desktop 3" is still "Desktop 3." Apple's API doesn't expose Space naming to any third-party app — there's no system-level hook to hang a label on.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Screen Time gets activated when an app launches and stays that way as long as the app is open; the clock keeps ticking even if the app is minimized or buried six windows deep on your desktop. To me, that makes it practically useless.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There's an app that deals with both of those irritants: &lt;a href="https://currentkey.com/"&gt;CurrentKey&lt;/a&gt; (formerly CurrentKey Stats) wraps every Space in a named, icon-coded "Room" you can jump to by hotkey or dropdown, then quietly logs how much time you actually spend in each one, broken down by app. The name lives in CurrentKey's own popover and menu bar, not inside Mission Control itself.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I wrote about CurrentKey a couple of years ago (&lt;a href="https://appaddict.app/post/currentkey-stats-a-triple-threat-app"&gt;CurrentKey Stats - A Triple Threat App&lt;/a&gt;, when it was working through a subscription model — an admitted turn-off for many. Today the app is free, although if you want to support the developer, Spencer Dailey, you can pay $3.99 to turn on a cosmetic layer that offers custom icon colors, any emoji as a Room icon, custom icon images, and banner images that pop up in a screen corner when you enter a Room. Those are nice to have but don't affect functionality. The basic (free) version has Room naming, hotkeys, switching, AppleScript triggers, and stats/export functionality. &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/currentkey-stats/id1456226992?mt=12"&gt;(App Store)&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Five Features, Well Done&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;AppleScript hooks on every Room switch.&lt;/strong&gt; This is the feature that separates CurrentKey from being just another desktop labeler — you can automatically fire a script the moment you enter or leave a Room, which means bringing a specific app forward, pausing a timer just by switching context or even something crazy, like triggering smart lights.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Time tracking scoped to foreground use, not just "app open."&lt;/strong&gt; Unlike Screen Time, which counts an app as active the whole time it's running, CurrentKey only counts minutes an app is actually in the foreground — closer to what a freelancer billing by the hour actually needs.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Per-Room, per-app breakdowns with CSV export.&lt;/strong&gt; Eleven charts, 30-day history, daily and weekly summaries, and a real export path if you want to reconcile hours against a client invoice instead of trusting a dashboard.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;Hotkey-driven Room switching, up to 16 per screen.&lt;/strong&gt; Mac Spaces already cap at 16 per display; CurrentKey lets you actually use that ceiling by making each one reachable without a three-finger swipe and a guess.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;
&lt;strong&gt;All data stays on-device.&lt;/strong&gt; No account, no cloud sync required to use the core app — export is opt-in, which matters if the whole point is separating "work" time from "distraction" time and you'd rather that stay local.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Alternatives&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://www.getspacejump.com/"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;SpaceJump&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; ($9.99 one-time after a 14-day trial) is the more direct competitor — it uses overlay windows to project custom Space name labels onto the Mission Control view itself (no SIP disable required), and it also tracks time per Space. It's not "true" system-level renaming either — Apple doesn't expose that to anyone — but the label appears inside Mission Control rather than in a separate popover, which is a real difference in feel from CurrentKey. Pricier, and it skips the AppleScript hooks.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/id/app/desktop-space-renamer/id6745852577?mt=12"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Desktop Space Renamer&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; is a lightweight, low-cost menu bar app that does the naming and emoji-labeling part of CurrentKey's job with none of the time-tracking or scripting depth — a fine choice if all you want is to stop guessing which Space is which.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;
&lt;a href="https://github.com/dado3212/spaces-renamer"&gt;&lt;strong&gt;spaces-renamer&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/a&gt; (free, open source) is the older, hackier route: a SIMBL-plugin-based renamer that predates Apple Silicon and reportedly doesn't work reliably on M1/M2 Macs or recent macOS versions. It's free, but effectively unmaintained for anyone on current hardware.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you use BetterTouchTool, and you know how to use it, you already have multi-Space switching, window snapping tied to specific Spaces, and gesture-triggered Mission Control previews as part of a much larger automation toolkit. You lose CurrentKey's purpose-built stats and per-Room AppleScript triggers.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who This Helps&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can use CurrentKey if your Mac already has more Spaces than you can honestly remember, and you want both the friction of switching between them and the accounting of time spent in them solved by one small, actively maintained, free utility with real scripting hooks. The AppleScript integration in particular is doing work other Space renaming apps don't.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who This Isn't For&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you want the Space name to actually show up inside Mission Control's swipe-up view rather than in a separate popover, CurrentKey won't scratch that itch — SpaceJump will, for the extra cost.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=CurrentKey,%20Removing%20Mac%20Friction%20Points%20with%20Space%20Naming%20and%20ScreenTime%20Info%20You%20Can%20Actually%20Use" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>Here are two Mac friction points:

• It's been 16 years since Mission Control was released, and "Desktop 3" is still "Desktop 3." Apple's API doesn't expose Space naming to any third-party app — there's no system-level hook to hang a label on.
• Screen Time gets activated when an...</summary>

3750w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;em&gt;TL;DR - Turn just about any collection of audiobook files (FLAC,WAV,MP3) into a single iPhone compatible M4B complete with metadata and chapters. Mac, $9.99, Solo dev&lt;/em&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;I've been listening to audiobooks since they were called books on tape. I progressed from there to CDs and then to miscellaneous downloads. These days, the gold standard format, at least for Apple fans, is audiobooks packaged as single M4B files regardless of the book's length, complete with chapters and metadata. That way you can stop and start listening without searching for your place, add bookmarks and get a description and info on the author and narrator. My go-to tool for audiobook conversion is AudioBo, from solo developer Vlad at OrsoLabs, available in the &lt;a href="https://apps.apple.com/us/app/audiobo-audiobook-maker/id6754019673?mt=12"&gt;Mac App Store&lt;/a&gt; for $9.99. It will turn a folder full of old MP3 files and assorted cruft into something you can listen to on your iPhone, iPad, Apple TV, and yes, even classic iPods. Length is no issue. If you've got a 60-hour doorstop fantasy novel, AudioBo can handle it.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;For a long time, Reddit has recommended Audiobook Builder, and it's fine, except for the part where it caps output length and forces you into multiple part files for anything long. That's not a workflow, that's a workaround. For the price of a Big Mac combo, you can get AudioBo which converts MP3, FLAC, WAV, and other common formats into polished audiobooks and simplifies management and playback for good.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Features&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The three selling points for AudioBo are:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Metadata Fetch&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;AudioBo pulls title, author, and cover art from Audible, Apple Books, and Google Books in one click. That's the tedious part of building an audiobook done for you.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Non-Destructive Editing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;You can adjust chapters and metadata on an existing M4B without re-encoding. That preserves audio quality and saves real time, since re-encoding a long file is not fast.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;No Length Forcing&lt;/strong&gt;&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Long-form audiobooks stay as one file instead of getting split into parts because the app couldn't handle the duration.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Intangibles&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;While researching AudioBo for this review, I found multiple instances where the developer has responded to feature requests in a thread and then shipped within days. To me, that's a pretty good sign that this app will be maintained going forward. I'm normally wary of App Store reviews because of astroturfing and vague "Good App!" posts, but reading through the reviews left for AudioBo is pretty convincing. The written reviews back it up with specifics rather than vague praise. "Far and away, the best audiobook conversion app I've found," one reviewer wrote. Another called it the "Current Gold Standard of Audiobook Converters on App Store." 9to5Mac gave it a full hands-on writeup, not a roundup mention, and the reviewer's (well-known Mac journalist, Bradley Chambers) verdict after testing it on several massive projects was direct: it delivers, and it's now his go-to.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Roadmap&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There are still a few features that the app needs. Currently it doesn't support batch/multi-instance processing. Opening a new window wipes the book you're currently working on, even mid-export. So, don't expect to dump your library in a folder and walk away. The good news is that the feature is coming, according to the dev. The only other hiccup is pretty specific: when re-encoding existing M4B files to go from stereo to mono or to change the bitrate, several people report having issues. That's not something I would ever do, so I haven't experienced it firsthand.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h2&gt;Who This is for&lt;/h2&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you're building or maintaining audiobooks on the Mac and you've hit Audiobook Builder's length ceiling, or you just want metadata fetching that doesn't require three separate lookups, AudioBo is the better option. It's Apple/M4B-focused only, so if you need Audible AAX/DRM handling or cross-platform output for Kobo or Kindle, this isn't that tool, and it isn't trying to be.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;$9.99 one-time, free demo on the &lt;a href="https://orsolabs.dev/audiobo/"&gt;developer's site&lt;/a&gt;. No subscription - something we all appreciate.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=AudioBo:%20The%20Audiobook%20Builder%20That%20Doesn" t make you choose parts and style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>
    <summary>TL;DR - Turn just about any collection of audiobook files (FLAC,WAV,MP3) into a single iPhone compatible M4B complete with metadata and chapters. Mac, $9.99, Solo dev

I've been listening to audiobooks since they were called books on tape. I progressed from there to CDs and then to miscellaneous downloads. These...</summary>

    <title>Finbar is an Indy Gem for Keyboard First Users</title>
    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" srcset="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFMZ0FXa0M0QUU2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--566037cccbef5dec0f18059f150ac6f098af6027/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg 361w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFLVkFta0NsUUk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--b11ebfa34111615cae03143e19175f25060c680c/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg 498w" sizes="(max-width: 672px) 100vw, 672px" loading="lazy" data-lightbox-url="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/blobs/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg" src="https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBKzNPQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--d43265948796601c8971e8eba8e2a9371a8a1b4f/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFLVkFta0NsUUk2Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--b11ebfa34111615cae03143e19175f25060c680c/CleanShot%202026-07-15%20at%2012.47.43.jpg" decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;In past lives, my bosses pressed me into using a few complex and complicated apps - mostly Adobe and Microsoft stuff, some AutoCAD. One thing they all have in common is crammed menu bars where what you are actually looking for seldom makes sense and when it does, it's buried three levels deep. Those are the ones that Microsoft likes to use as answers to questions on certification exams.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There's no shortage of specialty apps, like Paletro and automation tools like Raycast, Alfred and BetterTouchTool that try to address menu bar searches. Most of them are good at doing 70% of what it takes but they just never seem to get that final burst of polish it takes to solve the problem. That's where Finbar steps in. For $9.99, you get an app that sees every menu bar option, no matter how deep.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;Can't remember the name of what you're looking for? Finbar has fuzzy search.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;Use the same commands over and over? Finbar remembers that and surfaces them for you.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;Don't use part of the app? Exclude its menu choices from what you see to reduce clutter and simplify things.&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If your keyboard skills are equal to or greater than your clicking skills, take advantage of the free trial and test Finbar. &lt;strong&gt;Outline Mode&lt;/strong&gt; is the feature to try first--it transforms every menu bar into a keyboard-navigable tree, like Finder's sidebar. You can arrow through, expand/collapse, and commit without lifting your hands.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If your workflow isn't keyboard centric and you aren't regularly drilling into menu items, you don't need this. Use Raycast or Alfred. But, if your daily drivers include the apps I mention earlier, this should be an instabuy.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;$9.99, one-time purchase.&lt;/strong&gt; Free trial available. Download at &lt;a href="https://finbarapp.com/"&gt;finbarapp.com&lt;/a&gt; or via Homebrew (&lt;code&gt;brew install --cask finbar&lt;/code&gt;). Requires macOS Big Sur or later. Roey Biran--&lt;a href="https://x.com/finbarapp"&gt;@finbarapp&lt;/a&gt; on X--built this on the Unix principle of doing one thing well. It shows.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Finbar%20is%20an%20Indy%20Gem%20for%20Keyboard%20First%20Users" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

    <content type="html">&lt;figure class="attachment attachment--preview flex-col justify-center attachment--jpg"&gt;
    &lt;img class="lightbox__image strip-metadata lightbox__image" 800w, https://scribbles.page/rails/active_storage/representations/proxy/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaHBBL0RGQVE9PSIsImV4cCI6bnVsbCwicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--e75d0ed3971c8ece4c3de397af57e810c24c9ecf/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsibWVzc2FnZSI6IkJBaDdDRG9MWm05eWJXRjBTU0lJYW5CbkJqb0dSVlE2RkhKbGMybDZaVjkwYjE5c2FXMXBkRnNIYVFLNEEya0N1QU02Q25OaGRtVnlld2M2REhGMVlXeHBkSGxwV1RvS2MzUnlhWEJVIiwiZXhwIjpudWxsLCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--d936e114f03fdb2f8ce27b5d9aea18b88881243b/CleanShot%202026-07-11%20at%2015.45.41.jpg decoding="async"&gt;
&lt;/figure&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Apple, in its infinite wisdom, buries a great many popular system controls three layers deep in Settings, or worse, leaves them accessible only via the command line. Luckily, we have a community of indie developers who are pretty good at surfacing that stuff, building an app around it, and selling it for $5. An app for brightness. An app for the notch. An app to keep the Mac awake. An app to mute the mic. Then one day your menu bar has 40 icons in it and your login items are out of control.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;There's a relatively new, free and open-source app that takes the opposite approach. Currently sporting &lt;a href="https://github.com/ggbond268/MacTools"&gt;over 500 GitHub stars, Mac Tools&lt;/a&gt; folds more than 40 of those functions into a single menu bar icon. It's built natively in SwiftUI and AppKit; the functions run on native Mac architecture, not scripts. Brightness goes through CoreDisplay, audio through CoreAudio, and disk cleanup runs path verification before it deletes anything. That last one matters: a cleanup tool that checks its work before emptying folders is rarer than it should be.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;Check out the &lt;a href="https://mactools.ggbond.app"&gt;Mac Tools website.&lt;/a&gt; Mac Tools is available through Homebrew:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;pre data-language="javascript"&gt;brew tap ggbond268/mactools  &lt;br&gt;brew install --cask mactools&lt;br&gt;&lt;/pre&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What It Does&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The features break down into five groups. You enable the plugins for what you want and leave the rest turned off.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Display Control&lt;/strong&gt; -- resolution switching per monitor, DDC/CI brightness for external displays, True Tone, dark mode, Night Shift, display sleep, prevent sleep, notch hiding, and menu bar icon hiding. This group alone covers what most people buy three or four separate utilities to do.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;System Operations&lt;/strong&gt; -- Stage Manager toggle, system and microphone mute, disk cleanup, Xcode cleanup, eject all disks, empty trash, clear clipboard, lock screen, batch quit apps, and a fix for the "app is damaged and can't be opened" error, which is really just quarantine flag removal with a file picker instead of an &lt;code&gt;xattr&lt;/code&gt; command.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Efficiency Tools&lt;/strong&gt; -- three-finger middle click on the trackpad, a cleaning mode that blacks out the screen and locks input so you can wipe the keyboard, IP lookup, translation, global app hotkeys, a full-screen Launchpad replacement, Finder right-click enhancements, and a zsh config editor.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Monitoring Panel&lt;/strong&gt; -- CPU, GPU, memory, disk, network, and battery with one-hour history curves; keyboard, mouse, and app usage statistics; battery levels for the Mac plus Bluetooth peripherals and AirPods; fan control; and a charge limiter that defaults to 80 percent.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;&lt;strong&gt;Personalization&lt;/strong&gt; -- custom menu bar icons including GIF and MP4 animations, Launchpad appearance controls, 11 languages, and a plugin marketplace.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The plugin architecture is what keeps this from becoming bloatware. Everything can be enabled, hidden, or reordered, so the panel only shows what you actually use.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;What It Replaces&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;The point of Mac Tools is consolidation, not feature-for-feature parity with every indie tool it overlaps. Lunar is still the king of independent monitor control, but if you just need brightness adjustment, Mac Tools handles it. If Amphetamine is only in your Dock to stop the Mac from sleeping, Mac Tools does that too. Across a whole set of single-purpose categories, it's a credible replacement for:&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;ul&gt;
&lt;li value="1"&gt;a notch hider&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="2"&gt;a mic mute utility&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="3"&gt;an eject-all tool&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="4"&gt;Itsycal-style calendar duty&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="5"&gt;a Stats-style monitor&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="6"&gt;a fan controller&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="7"&gt;a charge limiter&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;li value="8"&gt;an app usage tracker&lt;/li&gt;
&lt;/ul&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;The Catch and a Reality Check&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;This is a relatively new app. After it appeared on GitHubDaily and in a Medium article, its popularity spiked fast. The developer's true identity is unknown; "ggbond268" is a pseudonym, and the project came out of the Chinese Mac community. The README is in Chinese, though the app itself is localized into English and ten other languages. That's not disqualifying on its own -- I run Chinese-built apps like Qspace regularly -- but it's the kind of context you want before you grant an app broad system access, not after.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;And several of these features do ask for broad access. Fan control installs a helper with admin rights. Disk cleanup deletes files. The middle-click feature uses an event tap. Quarantine removal is the kind of thing you want done carefully, not casually. The code being open and the app being native counts for a lot -- that's the whole argument for shipping as a public repo instead of a black box. What it doesn't have yet is a public security audit. Worth knowing before you install, not a reason to skip it outright.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;h3&gt;Is This For You?&lt;/h3&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you're comfortable installing from a Homebrew tap, you like open source, and your menu bar currently hosts a small orchestra of single-purpose utilities, Mac Tools is an easy experiment. It's free, it's light, and the plugin design means you can turn on three features and ignore the rest.&lt;/p&gt;

&lt;p&gt;If you'd rather pay for a mature tool with a support address and years of releases behind it, or handing admin rights to a young, pseudonymous project makes you itch, stick with the battle-tested standalones for now and check back in six months. Promising and early -- both are true at once.&lt;/p&gt;
&lt;p&gt;&lt;a href="mailto:lou@louplummer.lol?subject=Mac%20Tools%20Consolidates%20Your%20Utility%20Bloat%20%E2%80%94%20With%20One%20Catch" style="text-decoration: underline"&gt;✉️ Reply by email&lt;/a&gt;&lt;/p&gt;</content>

Luckily, we have a community of indie developers who are pretty good at surfacing that stuff, building an app around it, and selling...</summary>
